#### Processing the Data

```{r, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
#| code-fold: true

# Load necessary package
library(knitr)

# Set folder path

# Load the datasets
capex <- read.csv(file.path(data_path, "CAPEX.csv"))
fedfunds <- read.csv(file.path(data_path, "FEDFUNDS.csv"))
indeed_da <- read.csv(file.path(data_path, "indeed_data_analysis_job_postings.csv"))
pce <- read.csv(file.path(data_path, "PCE.csv"))
ppi_info <- read.csv(file.path(data_path, "PPI_Information.csv"))
unemployment_info <- read.csv(file.path(data_path, "Unemployment_Information.csv"))

# Convert date columns to Date
capex[, 1] <- as.Date(capex[, 1])
fedfunds[, 1] <- as.Date(fedfunds[, 1])
pce[, 1] <- as.Date(pce[, 1])
ppi_info[, 1] <- as.Date(ppi_info[, 1])
unemployment_info[, 1] <- as.Date(unemployment_info[, 1])

# Clean Indeed dataset separately because its date column is dateString
indeed_da$dateString <- as.Date(indeed_da$dateString)

# Keep only date and value columns
capex <- capex[, 1:2]
fedfunds <- fedfunds[, 1:2]
pce <- pce[, 1:2]
ppi_info <- ppi_info[, 1:2]
unemployment_info <- unemployment_info[, 1:2]

indeed_da <- indeed_da[, c("dateString", "value")]

# Rename columns for clarity
colnames(capex) <- c("Date", "CAPEX")
colnames(fedfunds) <- c("Date", "FedFundsRate")
colnames(indeed_da) <- c("Date", "DataAnalysisJobPostings")
colnames(pce) <- c("Date", "PCE")
```

The data need to convert to quaretly data. We will use interpolation.

```{r, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
#| code-fold: true
# Load necessary packages
library(knitr)
library(dplyr)
library(lubridate)

# Set folder path
data_path <- "DA_Jobs_vs_Econ"

# Load the datasets
capex <- read.csv(file.path(data_path, "CAPEX.csv"))
fedfunds <- read.csv(file.path(data_path, "FEDFUNDS.csv"))
indeed_da <- read.csv(file.path(data_path, "indeed_data_analysis_job_postings.csv"))
pce <- read.csv(file.path(data_path, "PCE.csv"))
ppi_info <- read.csv(file.path(data_path, "PPI_Information.csv"))
unemployment_info <- read.csv(file.path(data_path, "Unemployment_Information.csv"))

# Convert date columns to Date
capex[, 1] <- as.Date(capex[, 1])
fedfunds[, 1] <- as.Date(fedfunds[, 1])
pce[, 1] <- as.Date(pce[, 1])
ppi_info[, 1] <- as.Date(ppi_info[, 1])
unemployment_info[, 1] <- as.Date(unemployment_info[, 1])

# Clean Indeed dataset separately because its date column is dateString
indeed_da$dateString <- as.Date(indeed_da$dateString)

# Keep only date and value columns
capex <- capex[, 1:2]
fedfunds <- fedfunds[, 1:2]
pce <- pce[, 1:2]
ppi_info <- ppi_info[, 1:2]
unemployment_info <- unemployment_info[, 1:2]

indeed_da <- indeed_da %>%
  filter(
    countryCode == "US",
    sectorName == "Data & Analytics",
    postingType == "TOTAL"
  ) %>%
  select(dateString, value)

# Rename columns for clarity
colnames(capex) <- c("Date", "CAPEX")
colnames(fedfunds) <- c("Date", "FedFundsRate")
colnames(indeed_da) <- c("Date", "DataAnalysisJobPostings")
colnames(pce) <- c("Date", "PCE")
colnames(ppi_info) <- c("Date", "PPIInformation")
colnames(unemployment_info) <- c("Date", "UnemploymentRate")

# Function to convert any dataset to quarterly data
to_quarterly <- function(df) {
  df %>%
    mutate(
      Date = floor_date(Date, unit = "quarter")
    ) %>%
    group_by(Date) %>%
    summarise(
      across(
        .cols = where(is.numeric),
        .fns = ~ mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE)
      ),
      .groups = "drop"
    )
}

# Convert all datasets to quarterly frequency
capex_q <- to_quarterly(capex)
fedfunds_q <- to_quarterly(fedfunds)
indeed_da_q <- to_quarterly(indeed_da)
pce_q <- to_quarterly(pce)
ppi_info_q <- to_quarterly(ppi_info)
unemployment_info_q <- to_quarterly(unemployment_info)

# Merge quarterly datasets using only the common quarterly time period
merged_data <- Reduce(
  function(x, y) merge(x, y, by = "Date", all = FALSE),
  list(
    capex_q,
    fedfunds_q,
    indeed_da_q,
    pce_q,
    ppi_info_q,
    unemployment_info_q
  )
)

# Sort by Date
merged_data <- merged_data %>%
  arrange(Date)

# Remove any rows with missing values
merged_data <- merged_data %>%
  filter(if_all(-Date, ~ !is.na(.x)))

# Display common time period
cat(
  "Common quarterly time period:",
  as.character(min(merged_data$Date)),
  "to",
  as.character(max(merged_data$Date)),
  "\n"
)

# Display number of quarterly observations
cat("Number of quarterly observations:", nrow(merged_data), "\n")

# Display the first few rows
kable(
  head(merged_data),
  caption = "Merged Quarterly Dataset: Common Time Period Only"
)
```

### Fitting the model using ’auto.arima()`

We are using `auto.arima()` function to fit the ARIMAX model. Here we are predicting Total vehicle using the other variables. Remember all variables are time series and the exogenous variables in this case are Vehicle Miles Traveled, Consumer Price Index for New Vehicles, Finance Rate on Consumer Installment Loans, 60-Month Loan and Loan availability (MVLOAS).

```{r, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
#| code-fold: true


# Load necessary packages
library(forecast)
library(lubridate)

# Use merged quarterly dataset
df <- merged_data

# Make sure data are sorted by Date
df <- df[order(df$Date), ]

# Remove rows with missing values
df <- na.omit(df)

# Get start year and quarter from the first date
start_year <- year(min(df$Date))
start_quarter <- quarter(min(df$Date))

# Convert to time series object
# Quarterly data: frequency = 4
df.ts <- ts(
  df[, -1],
  start = c(start_year, start_quarter),
  frequency = 4
)

# Define the dependent variable
# Here we are modeling Data Analysis job postings
y <- df.ts[, "DataAnalysisJobPostings"]

# Define external regressors
# All variables except DataAnalysisJobPostings
xreg <- df.ts[, c(
  "CAPEX",
  "FedFundsRate",
  "PCE",
  "PPIInformation",
  "UnemploymentRate"
)]

# Fit the ARIMA model with external regressors
fit <- auto.arima(y, xreg = xreg)

# Display model summary
summary(fit)

# Model diagnostics
checkresiduals(fit)
```

The `auto.arima()` fits a Regression with ARIMA(0,0,0)(1,0,0)[4] errors  . The ACF plot shows high correlation in the residuals meaning that basic Machine Learning models are not enough to accounter the high serial correlation in time series variables.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Fitting the model manually

Instead of using the `auto.arima()` fucntion, let's fit the model manually. First let's fit the regression model to analyse the how these economical variables affect total vehicle sales in the US.

```{r, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
#| code-fold: true

# Fit a linear regression model
model <- lm(
  DataAnalysisJobPostings ~ CAPEX + FedFundsRate + PCE + PPIInformation + UnemploymentRate ,
  data = df
)

# Fit a linear regression model
model2 <- lm(
  DataAnalysisJobPostings ~ CAPEX  + PCE,
  data = df
)

model3 <- lm(
  DataAnalysisJobPostings ~ CAPEX  + FedFundsRate,
  data = df
)

model4 <- lm(
  DataAnalysisJobPostings ~ PPIInformation  + FedFundsRate,
  data = df
)

model5 <- lm(
  DataAnalysisJobPostings ~ PCE  + FedFundsRate,
  data = df
)

model6 <- lm(
  DataAnalysisJobPostings ~ CAPEX  + PPIInformation,
  data = df
)

# Store all models in a list
models <- list(
  Full_Model = model,
  CAPEX_PCE = model2,
  CAPEX_FedFundsRate = model3,
  PPIInformation_FedFundsRate = model4,
  PCE_FedFundsRate = model5,
  CAPEX_PPIInformation = model6
)

# Display full regression summaries
lapply(models, summary)


```

From the regression model, all variables are statistically significant, indicating that **finance rates, loans, CPI, and miles traveled** have a meaningful impact on total vehicle sales. This suggests that changes in these factors directly influence vehicle sales trends.

Moreover, the residuals exhibit a high correlation, indicating significant serial correlation that remains unexplained. This suggests that traditional machine learning models may struggle to fully capture the underlying temporal patterns in these time series variables.

```{r, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
#| code-fold: true

# Load necessary packages
library(forecast)
library(lubridate)
library(ggplot2)

# Make sure df is sorted by Date
df <- df[order(df$Date), ]

# Get the starting year and quarter from your actual dataset
start_year <- year(min(df$Date))
start_quarter <- quarter(min(df$Date))

# Store all models in a list
models <- list(
  Full_Model = model,
  CAPEX_PCE = model2,
  CAPEX_FedFundsRate = model3,
  PPIInformation_FedFundsRate = model4,
  PCE_FedFundsRate = model5,
  CAPEX_PPIInformation = model6
)

# Function to create residual time series
make_residual_ts <- function(model_object) {
  ts(
    residuals(model_object),
    start = c(start_year, start_quarter),
    frequency = 4
  )
}

# Create ACF and PACF plots for each model
for (model_name in names(models)) {
  
  res.fit <- make_residual_ts(models[[model_name]])
  
  print(
    ggAcf(res.fit) +
      ggtitle(paste("ACF of Residuals:", model_name))
  )
  
  print(
    ggPacf(res.fit) +
      ggtitle(paste("PACF of Residuals:", model_name))
  )
}

```

To address the remaining serial correlation in the residuals, we will fit an **ARIMA or SARIMA model** to the residuals of our regression model. This approach creates an **ensemble model**, where the regression model captures the linear relationships, and the time series model accounts for the unexplained serial correlation in the residuals.

## Lag Plots

```{r}
# Load necessary packages
library(forecast)
library(plotly)
library(ggplot2)
library(lubridate)

# Make sure df is sorted by Date
df <- df[order(df$Date), ]

# Remove missing values
df <- na.omit(df)

# Get start year and quarter from your actual dataset
start_year <- year(min(df$Date))
start_quarter <- quarter(min(df$Date))

# Variables used across the 6 models
variables <- c(
  "DataAnalysisJobPostings",
  "CAPEX",
  "FedFundsRate",
  "PCE",
  "PPIInformation",
  "UnemploymentRate"
)

# Cleaner names for plot titles and axis labels
variable_labels <- c(
  DataAnalysisJobPostings = "Data Analysis Job Postings",
  CAPEX = "CAPEX",
  FedFundsRate = "Federal Funds Rate",
  PCE = "PCE",
  PPIInformation = "PPI Information",
  UnemploymentRate = "Unemployment Rate"
)

# Function to create lag plot for one variable
create_lag_plot <- function(var_name, lags = 9) {
  
  ts_var <- ts(
    df[[var_name]],
    start = c(start_year, start_quarter),
    frequency = 4
  )
  
  p <- gglagplot(
    ts_var,
    do.lines = FALSE,
    lags = lags
  ) +
    ggtitle(paste("Lag Plots for", variable_labels[var_name])) +
    xlab(paste("Lagged", variable_labels[var_name])) +
    ylab(paste("Current", variable_labels[var_name])) +
    theme_minimal()
  
  ggplotly(p)
}

# Create lag plots
lag_plot_job_postings <- create_lag_plot("DataAnalysisJobPostings")
lag_plot_capex <- create_lag_plot("CAPEX")
lag_plot_fedfunds <- create_lag_plot("FedFundsRate")
lag_plot_pce <- create_lag_plot("PCE")
lag_plot_ppi <- create_lag_plot("PPIInformation")
lag_plot_unemployment <- create_lag_plot("UnemploymentRate")

lag_plot_job_postings
lag_plot_capex
lag_plot_fedfunds
lag_plot_pce
lag_plot_ppi
lag_plot_unemployment
```

## ACF Plots

```{r}
# Load necessary packages
library(forecast)
library(plotly)
library(ggplot2)
library(lubridate)
library(htmltools)

# Make sure df is sorted by Date
df <- df[order(df$Date), ]

# Remove missing values
df <- na.omit(df)

# Get start year and quarter from your actual dataset
start_year <- year(min(df$Date))
start_quarter <- quarter(min(df$Date))

# Variables used across the 6 models
variables <- c(
  "DataAnalysisJobPostings",
  "CAPEX",
  "FedFundsRate",
  "PCE",
  "PPIInformation",
  "UnemploymentRate"
)

# Cleaner names for plot titles and axis labels
variable_labels <- c(
  DataAnalysisJobPostings = "Data Analysis Job Postings",
  CAPEX = "CAPEX",
  FedFundsRate = "Federal Funds Rate",
  PCE = "PCE",
  PPIInformation = "PPI Information",
  UnemploymentRate = "Unemployment Rate"
)

# Function to create ACF plot for one variable
create_acf_plot <- function(var_name, lag_max = 9) {
  
  ts_var <- ts(
    df[[var_name]],
    start = c(start_year, start_quarter),
    frequency = 4
  )
  
  p <- ggAcf(
    ts_var,
    lag.max = lag_max
  ) +
    ggtitle(paste("ACF Plot for", variable_labels[var_name])) +
    xlab("Lag in Quarters") +
    ylab("Autocorrelation") +
    theme_minimal()
  
  ggplotly(p)
}

# Create ACF plots
acf_plot_job_postings <- create_acf_plot("DataAnalysisJobPostings")
acf_plot_capex <- create_acf_plot("CAPEX")
acf_plot_fedfunds <- create_acf_plot("FedFundsRate")
acf_plot_pce <- create_acf_plot("PCE")
acf_plot_ppi <- create_acf_plot("PPIInformation")
acf_plot_unemployment <- create_acf_plot("UnemploymentRate")
```

<!-- The **Q-Q Plot** indicates that the residuals follow a near-normal distribution, with minor deviations at the tails, which is typical in time series data. -->

<!-- The **Ljung-Box Test** p-values remain mostly above the 0.05 significance level, implying a nearly good fit. -->

<!-- **Coefficient Significance**: For the first model the coefficient of sma1 is not significant at 5% Significance level, but for the second model all variables are significant. -->

<!-- With the parameters from the model: -->

<!-- $$\Phi_P\left(B^{12}\right) \varphi(B) \nabla_{12}^{D=0} \nabla^{d=1} n_t=\Theta_Q\left(B^{12}\right) \theta(B) w_t$$ $$(1-B) (1-\phi_1 B-\phi_2 B^2) n_t=\left(1+\theta_1 B+ \theta_2 B^2)(1+\Theta B^{12}\right) w_t$$ $$(1-B) (1+0.1728B+0.7576 B^2) n_t=\left(1+0.5832B-0.2784 B^2)(1+0.1668 B^{12}\right) w_t$$ -->
